title: Gauge-invariant thermodynamics of a finite-time quantum Otto engine
authors: Midana Baial Sambú, Thiago R. de Oliveira, Lucas C. Céleri
abstract: We investigate a finite-time quantum Otto engine within the framework of gauge-invariant quantum thermodynamics, using the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model as the working medium. In this formulation, thermodynamic quantities are defined on equivalence classes of thermodynamically indistinguishable states, leading naturally to gauge-invariant notions of work, heat, entropy, and efficiency. We derive explicit expressions for these quantities and show that the usual work performed during the unitary strokes decomposes into an invariant contribution, associated with changes in the instantaneous energy spectrum and populations, and a coherent contribution arising from finite-time quantum coherences. This decomposition induces the corresponding splittings of engine efficiency and entropy production, providing a geometric interpretation of finite-time irreversibility and clarifying the role of coherence in work extraction. By analyzing the cycle's dependence on driving speed and system size, we identify the engine's operating region and investigate the influence of criticality. We show that crossing the critical region substantially reduces the parameter space in which the cycle operates as a heat engine. At the same time, whenever the engine condition remains satisfied, the discrepancy between the conventional and gauge-invariant descriptions becomes strongly suppressed, indicating that the gauge-invariant sector predominantly carries the extracted work. These results establish a direct connection between gauge-invariant thermodynamics, finite-time irreversibility, and work extraction in many-body quantum thermal machines.
summary: This theoretical paper develops a gauge-invariant framework to analyze thermodynamics in finite-time quantum Otto engines using the LMG model. It successfully decomposes total work and entropy production into components associated with population changes and quantum coherences. This clarifies the role of coherence in irreversible processes, showing how the invariant sector captures the essential extracted work.
main_problem: The paper addresses how to formulate quantum thermodynamics for finite-time processes by defining thermodynamic quantities that are invariant under transformations preserving the mean energy (gauge invariance). It aims to separate work extraction into contributions from population changes and quantum coherences.
main_result: A gauge-invariant decomposition of work and entropy production is derived, showing that the extracted work can be split into an 'invariant contribution' related to energy spectrum changes and a 'coherent contribution.'
method: The authors employ a gauge-invariant thermodynamic framework by defining observables on equivalence classes of states, analyzing the Otto cycle using the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick model.
model_or_system: The working medium is modeled by the Lipkin-Meshkov-Glick (LMG) Hamiltonian, which describes collective angular momentum operators for spin-1/2 particles. The analysis focuses on a finite-time quantum Otto engine cycle.
key_observables: Gauge-invariant work ($W_{	ext{inv}}$), heat, entropy production ($\Sigma$), and the ratio $\kappa$ comparing usual vs. gauge-invariant work.
important_parameters: Driving speed (related to time dependence of fields), system size ($N=2j$), and critical parameters associated with the LMG model ($\delta_c = \gamma_x$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that thermodynamic quantities can be robustly defined via gauge invariance, particularly when only energy measurements are accessible.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the gauge-invariant formalism, applies it to the LMG model describing an Otto engine cycle, derives explicit decompositions for work and entropy production ($\Sigma = \Sigma_{	ext{pop}} + \Sigma_{	ext{coh}}$), and analyzes how these quantities behave near critical points.
why_interesting: The systematic separation of coherence effects from classical thermodynamic contributions in non-equilibrium quantum engines provides a powerful, general tool for understanding work extraction beyond standard energy conservation laws.
